parts.text: No one would have guessed
that this bedraggled creature
parts.meaning: that this wet and messy person

parts.text: had once been a proud and immaculately groomed woman.
parts.meaning: was once a proud, perfectly neat woman

sentences.grammar: "Had once been" shows a time before the past moment of the story.

sentences.context: For the girls' faces were so blank, and their bodies so still, they could have been dolls.
sentences.simple: The girls' faces showed no feeling and their bodies did not move, so they looked like dolls.
sentences.main: ... were so blank, and ... so still, they could have been dolls.

parts.text: For
the girls' faces were so blank,
and their bodies so still,
parts.meaning: and their bodies were so still

parts.text: they could have been dolls.

sentences.grammar: The second "were" is left out; "so ... (that)" gives the result.

sentences.context: Mr. Ebony gave Charlie a look of such overwhelming hatred, Charlie had to step back, dizzy with shock.
sentences.simple: Mr. Ebony looked at Charlie with so much hate that Charlie had to step back.
sentences.main: ... a look of such overwhelming hatred, Charlie had to step back ...

parts.text: Mr. Ebony gave Charlie a look of such overwhelming hatred,
parts.meaning: Mr. Ebony looked at Charlie with so much hate

parts.text: Charlie had to step back,
parts.meaning: that Charlie had to move back

parts.text: dizzy with shock.
parts.meaning: feeling faint because of the shock

sentences.grammar: "Such + noun (that) + result": the word "that" is often left out.

sentences.context: Charlie was not the sort of boy to hold back when he saw something interesting.
sentences.simple: When Charlie saw something interesting, he always wanted to look at it.
sentences.main: Charlie was not the sort of boy to ...

parts.text: Charlie was not the sort of boy
parts.meaning: Charlie was not a boy who would

parts.text: to hold back
when he saw something interesting.

sentences.grammar: "Not the sort of person to + verb" describes someone's character.

sentences.context: If it were true that the de Greys had always wanted to adopt a child, as they said, then why had they only just now got around to it?
sentences.simple: If the de Greys really always wanted a child, why did they wait so long to adopt one?
sentences.main: If it were true that ..., then why had they ...?

parts.text: If it were true
that the de Greys had always wanted to adopt a child,
parts.meaning: that they always wanted a child

parts.text: as they said,
then why had they only just now got around to it?
parts.meaning: why did they only do it now

sentences.grammar: "If it were true" shows that Billy doubts it. "Get around to" = finally do something after a long time.

sentences.context: He was now trapped in the Passing House, and the kind parents he had longed for were nothing more than coldhearted villains with extremely unpleasant powers.
sentences.simple: Billy was stuck in the Passing House, and the kind parents he wanted were really cruel people with nasty magic.
sentences.main: ... the kind parents he had longed for were nothing more than ...

parts.text: He was now trapped in the Passing House,
and the kind parents he had longed for
parts.meaning: the kind parents he had wanted so much

parts.text: were nothing more than coldhearted villains
with extremely unpleasant powers.

sentences.grammar: "He had longed for" is a relative clause without "that". "Nothing more than" = only.

sentences.context: Vivienne Vertigo (or Viva Valery, as she was known in the movies) might have been a film star, but this had never prevented her from being a kind and considerate mother.
sentences.simple: Olivia's mother was a film star, but she was still a kind and caring mother.
sentences.main: ... might have been a film star, but this had never prevented her from being ...

parts.text: Vivienne Vertigo
(or Viva Valery, as she was known in the movies)
parts.meaning: her film name was Viva Valery

parts.text: might have been a film star,
parts.job: might have been = although she was

parts.text: but this had never prevented her from being a kind and considerate mother.
parts.meaning: but she was still kind and caring

sentences.grammar: "Might have been ..., but ..." admits one fact before showing a contrast.

sentences.context: Did it count, he wondered, if you told a dog the things you could tell no one else?
sentences.simple: Billy asked himself whether telling a dog his secrets would break his oath.
sentences.main: Did it count, ... if you told a dog the things ...?

parts.text: Did it count,
he wondered,
if you told a dog
the things you could tell no one else?
parts.meaning: the secrets you could not tell anyone

sentences.grammar: "He wondered" can go in the middle of the question. "Count" here = matter, be included.

sentences.context: Who would have thought a gloomy old castle like that could have been a nice family home?
sentences.simple: Nobody would imagine that such a dark old castle was once a happy home.
sentences.main: Who would have thought ... could have been ...?

parts.text: Who would have thought
a gloomy old castle like that
could have been a nice family home?

sentences.grammar: "Who would have thought ...?" is a question that means "It is very surprising that ...".

sentences.context: Miss Chrystal sprinted across the grounds faster than Charlie would have thought possible.
sentences.simple: Miss Chrystal ran across the grounds much faster than Charlie expected.
sentences.main: ... faster than Charlie would have thought possible.

parts.text: Miss Chrystal sprinted across the grounds
faster than Charlie would have thought possible.
parts.meaning: faster than he expected she could

sentences.grammar: "Faster than ... would have thought possible" = surprisingly fast.

sentences.context: She didn't like eating with visitors, especially Miss Ingledew, whom she imagined was chasing her brother, though anyone could have told her that it was the other way around.
sentences.simple: She thought Miss Ingledew was chasing Paton, but really Paton was chasing Miss Ingledew.
sentences.main: ..., whom she imagined was chasing her brother, though ... it was the other way around.

parts.text: She didn't like eating with visitors,
parts.meaning: she disliked having guests at meals

parts.text: especially Miss Ingledew,
whom she imagined was chasing her brother,
parts.meaning: who, she thought, wanted to win Paton's love

parts.text: though anyone could have told her that it was the other way around.
parts.meaning: but really it was Paton who loved Julia

sentences.grammar: "The other way around" = the opposite. ("Whom" here is used where "who" would be more correct.)

sentences.context: But Uncle Paton and Miss Ingledew stepped into the house and introduced themselves as though Alice were a perfectly normal person, so Charlie decided to follow them.
sentences.simple: Paton and Julia behaved as if Alice was a completely ordinary person, so Charlie went in too.
sentences.main: ... as though Alice were a perfectly normal person, so Charlie decided ...

parts.text: But Uncle Paton and Miss Ingledew stepped into the house
and introduced themselves
as though Alice were a perfectly normal person,
parts.meaning: as if she was quite ordinary

parts.text: so Charlie decided to follow them.

sentences.grammar: "As though + were" describes how something seems, even if it may not be true.

sentences.context: Banging your nose on something you can't see is very frightening for a dog, and Charlie didn't know how to describe a force field in animal language.
sentences.simple: It is very scary for a dog to hit its nose on something invisible, and Charlie could not explain a force field to a dog.
sentences.main: Banging your nose on something you can't see is very frightening ...

parts.text: Banging your nose on something you can't see
parts.meaning: hitting your nose on an invisible thing

parts.text: is very frightening for a dog,
parts.meaning: is very scary for a dog

parts.text: and Charlie didn't know how to describe a force field in animal language.
parts.meaning: and Charlie could not explain it in a dog's language

sentences.grammar: An -ing clause can be the subject of a sentence: "Banging your nose ... is frightening."

sentences.context: Florence and Usher de Grey slept very soundly proving that the old saying, "The wicked never sleep," can hardly be true.
sentences.simple: The de Greys slept deeply, which shows that the saying "bad people never sleep" is not true.
sentences.main: ... slept very soundly proving that the old saying ... can hardly be true.

parts.text: Florence and Usher de Grey slept very soundly
proving that the old saying, "The wicked never sleep,"
can hardly be true.

sentences.grammar: An -ing clause can show the result of the main clause. "Can hardly be" = is almost certainly not.

sentences.context: No one could have said for sure how long the battle raged, for time seemed to hold its breath until the radiant mist began to fade and the last tall figure vanished.
sentences.simple: Nobody knew how long the fight lasted; time seemed to stop until the mist and the spirits disappeared.
sentences.main: No one could have said for sure how long ..., for time seemed to hold its breath until ...

parts.text: No one could have said for sure
how long the battle raged,
parts.meaning: how long the fight went on

parts.text: for time seemed to hold its breath
until the radiant mist began to fade and the last tall figure vanished.
parts.meaning: until the mist and the spirits went away

sentences.grammar: "For" at the start of a clause can mean "because" (literary). "Time held its breath" is a picture: time seemed to stop.

sentences.context: The three boys stood in silence and watched the stately creature cropping the grass.
sentences.simple: The boys watched the beautiful horse eating grass without speaking.
sentences.main: The three boys ... watched the stately creature cropping the grass.

parts.text: The three boys stood in silence
and watched the stately creature
parts.meaning: and looked at the noble animal

parts.text: cropping the grass.

sentences.grammar: "Watch someone doing something" = see an action while it is happening. "Crop" = (of an animal) bite off and eat grass.

sentences.context: Just for a second, Charlie caught himself wondering if he should have given this adventure a little more thought before leaping into the dark — or onto a horse's back.
sentences.simple: For a moment Charlie wondered if he should have thought more before starting this adventure.
sentences.main: Charlie caught himself wondering if he should have given ... more thought before leaping ...

parts.text: Just for a second,
Charlie caught himself wondering
parts.meaning: Charlie suddenly noticed he was wondering

parts.text: if he should have given this adventure a little more thought
parts.meaning: if it would have been better to think more

parts.text: before leaping into the dark — or onto a horse's back.
parts.meaning: before jumping into danger (and onto a horse)

sentences.grammar: "Should have done" talks about a better choice in the past. "Leap into the dark" = do something risky without knowing what will happen.

sentences.context: Nothing is improbable to one who cannot remember his own life,
sentences.simple: When you cannot remember your own life, anything seems possible.
sentences.main: Nothing is improbable to one who ...

parts.text: Nothing is improbable
to one who cannot remember his own life,
parts.meaning: for a person who has lost his memory

sentences.grammar: "One who" is a formal way of saying "a person who".

sentences.context: Charlie felt as though there were a lead weight on his chest.
sentences.simple: Charlie felt so sad that it was like something heavy pressing on his chest.
sentences.main: Charlie felt as though there were ...

parts.text: Charlie felt
as though there were a lead weight on his chest.
parts.meaning: as if something very heavy was pressing on his chest

sentences.grammar: "Lead" (pronounced "led") is a heavy metal. A "lead weight" is a picture of great sadness.

sentences.context: If Albert was shocked, he didn't show it.
sentences.simple: Albert may have been shocked, but his face showed nothing.
sentences.main: If Albert was shocked, he didn't show it.

parts.text: If Albert was shocked,
he didn't show it.

sentences.grammar: "If ..., he didn't show it" means: maybe he felt it, but nobody could see.

sentences.context: You made yourself believe you'd find your father.
sentences.simple: You persuaded yourself that you would find your father.
sentences.main: You made yourself believe ...

parts.text: You made yourself believe
you'd find your father.
parts.meaning: that you would find your father

sentences.grammar: "Make yourself believe something" = try hard to believe it because you want it to be true.

sentences.context: You've come to see me. It's not too late.
sentences.simple: You have come to visit me, so there is still time.
sentences.main: It's not too late.

parts.text: You've come to see me.
parts.meaning: you have come to visit me

parts.text: It's not too late.

sentences.grammar: "It's not too late" = there is still time to do something.

sentences.context: She didn't look back, and her disappearance was just that, a melting into thin air, as if she hadn't really been there at all.
sentences.simple: She did not look back. She disappeared completely, as if she had never been there.
sentences.main: ..., as if she hadn't ...

parts.text: She didn't look back,
and her disappearance was just that,
parts.meaning: her going away was really a vanishing

parts.text: a melting into thin air,
parts.job: melting into thin air = disappearing completely

parts.text: as if she hadn't really been there at all.
parts.meaning: as though she had never been there

sentences.grammar: "As if + past perfect" describes something that seems true but is not.

sentences.context: She had the upper hand, so she thought.
sentences.simple: She believed she was in control, but she was wrong.
sentences.main: ..., so she thought.

parts.text: She had the upper hand,
parts.job: have the upper hand = be in control

parts.text: so she thought.
parts.job: so + subject + thought = that is what she believed (but she was wrong)
parts.meaning: or that is what she believed

sentences.grammar: "So she thought" at the end shows that she was wrong.

sentences.context: Fidelio's excited swagger made him nervous.
sentences.simple: Fidelio's proud, excited way of walking made Charlie nervous.
sentences.main: make + object + adjective

parts.text: Fidelio's excited swagger
made him nervous.

sentences.grammar: "Make someone nervous" = cause someone to feel nervous.

sentences.context: The two men were oblivious to the noise in the main part of the school.
sentences.simple: The two men did not notice the noise in the rest of the school.
sentences.main: be oblivious to ...

parts.text: The two men were oblivious to
parts.meaning: the two men did not notice

parts.text: the noise in the main part of the school.
parts.meaning: the noise in the rest of the school

sentences.grammar: "Be oblivious to something" = not notice it at all.

sentences.context: Better sign twice. Your grandfather appears to be out for the count.
sentences.simple: You had better sign twice. Your grandfather seems to be unconscious.
sentences.main: Better + verb

parts.text: Better sign twice.
Your grandfather appears to be out for the count.
parts.job: appear to be = seem to be

sentences.grammar: "Better sign twice" is short for "You had better sign twice."

sentences.context: I thought you would like to know that it was a success — except for one thing.
sentences.simple: I thought you would want to know it worked, except for one problem.
sentences.main: I thought you would like to know that ...

parts.text: I thought you would like to know
parts.meaning: I thought you would want to know

parts.text: that it was a success
— except for one thing.

sentences.grammar: "I thought you would like to know" is a polite way to begin giving news.

sentences.context: On Tuesday morning, Mr. Ebony and Mr. Wright had been inexplicably released.
sentences.simple: On Tuesday morning the two men were set free, and no one could explain why.
sentences.main: had been + past participle

parts.text: On Tuesday morning,
Mr. Ebony and Mr. Wright had been inexplicably released.
parts.meaning: the two men were set free for no clear reason

sentences.grammar: "Had been released" is the past perfect passive: someone set them free earlier.

sentences.context: Paton was reading about a place he'd known as a child, a place he had come to remember with horror.
sentences.simple: Paton was reading about a place he knew as a child. Now he remembered it with horror.
sentences.main: ..., a place he had ...

parts.text: Paton was reading about a place
parts.meaning: Paton was reading about a place

parts.text: he'd known as a child,
parts.meaning: that he had known when he was a child

parts.text: a place he had come to remember with horror.
parts.job: come to + verb = slowly begin to
parts.meaning: a place he now remembered with horror

sentences.grammar: The second "a place" repeats the idea to add more information about it.

sentences.context: Gabriel was sitting up, but he looked thin and peaked.
sentences.simple: Gabriel was sitting up in bed, but he looked thin and ill.

parts.text: Gabriel was sitting up,
parts.meaning: Gabriel was sitting up in bed

parts.text: but he looked thin and peaked.
parts.job: look + adjective; peaked = pale and ill
parts.meaning: but he seemed thin and pale

sentences.grammar: "Peaked" (said "PEEK-id") means looking pale and ill.

sentences.context: Uncle Paton said it would be foolhardy to use the Filbert Street house for a meeting.
sentences.simple: Paton said it would be silly and risky to meet at the Filbert Street house.
sentences.main: it would be + adjective + to ...

parts.text: Uncle Paton said
it would be foolhardy
parts.meaning: it would be silly and risky

parts.text: to use the Filbert Street house for a meeting.
parts.meaning: to meet at the house on Filbert Street

sentences.grammar: "It would be foolhardy to ..." = it would be a silly risk to ...

sentences.context: Wherever they were when Charlie looked at their photos
sentences.simple: No matter where those people were, when Charlie looked at their photos they would see his face near them.
sentences.grammar: Wherever they were comes first and names the place, and the rest of the sentence says what those people would see.

smarten yourself up.meaning: Make himself look neater and cleaner.
smarten yourself up.usageNote: You only need to understand it here.

in his stride.meaning: "Take something in your stride" = deal with something strange or difficult calmly, without getting upset.
in his stride.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

jumped out of his skin.meaning: "Jump out of your skin" = get a very big fright.
jumped out of his skin.example: nearly jumped out of his skin.
jumped out of his skin.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

rolling her eyes.meaning: "Roll your eyes" = turn your eyes upward to show you are annoyed or not surprised.
rolling her eyes.example: Olivia rolling her eyes at him
rolling her eyes.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

on their tails.meaning: (Informal) Following them closely all the time.
on their tails.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

perked up.example: who had perked up a bit.
perked up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

ward off.meaning: Keep something bad away; stop it from hurting you.
ward off.example: as if to ward off a blow
ward off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

my foot.meaning: (Informal) Used after repeating someone's words to show you don't believe them.
my foot.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

to say the least.meaning: Said to show that the truth is even stronger than your words.
to say the least.example: It's a little worrying, to say the least.
to say the least.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

in a bit of a jam.example: I'm in a bit of a jam.
in a bit of a jam.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

not a clue.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

held his ground.meaning: "Hold your ground" = not move back, although you want to.
held his ground.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

bolt upright.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

clear as mud.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

a cat may look at a queen.meaning: An old saying: even an unimportant person may look at an important one.
a cat may look at a queen.example: A cat may look at a queen,
a cat may look at a queen.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

like getting water out of a stone.example: like getting water out of a stone.
like getting water out of a stone.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

last but not least.meaning: Said before the last person or thing in a list, to show that it is just as important.
last but not least.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

pull himself together.meaning: Become calm again after being upset or surprised.
pull himself together.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

out of luck.meaning: Unlucky; not able to get what you want.
out of luck.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

sprang into action.meaning: "Spring into action" = suddenly start doing something quickly.
sprang into action.example: Children sprang into action like clockwork.
sprang into action.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

stuck with me.meaning: "Be stuck with someone" = have to accept someone you do not want.
stuck with me.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

under his breath.meaning: Very quietly, so others can't hear.
under his breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

cover for.meaning: Help someone by hiding the fact that they are not where they should be.
cover for.example: Can you cover for me if the matron comes in?
cover for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

at ease.example: We want to put the boy at ease.
at ease.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

none of your business.meaning: It is not something you should know about. (Rude.)
none of your business.example: "None of your business," snapped his great-aunt.
none of your business.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

get away with.meaning: Do something wrong or unfair and not be stopped or punished.
get away with.example: How did the Bloors get away with it?
get away with.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

dash Billy's hopes.meaning: Destroy his hopes; make what he hoped for impossible.
dash Billy's hopes.example: He didn't want to dash Billy's hopes
dash Billy's hopes.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

you're on.meaning: (1) (Informal) Agreed; I accept your plan. (2) Used in the normal way ("You're on your own now").
you're on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

bet your life on it.example: you can bet your life on it.
bet your life on it.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

without a backward glance.meaning: Without looking back, as if not caring.
without a backward glance.example: she strode away without a backward glance.
without a backward glance.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

by all accounts.example: He's a very knowledgeable gentleman, by all accounts.
by all accounts.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

signed him over.meaning: Give something to someone by signing a paper.
signed him over.example: His aunt just signed him over
signed him over.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

make yourself at home.meaning: Relax and feel comfortable, as if this were your own home.
make yourself at home.example: you make yourself at home, Billy.
make yourself at home.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

turned on her heels.meaning: "Turn on your heel" = turn around suddenly and walk away.
turned on her heels.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

egging him on.meaning: "Egg someone on" = encourage someone to do something bad or silly.
egging him on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

as big as saucers.meaning: (Of eyes) very wide open, because of surprise or fear.
as big as saucers.example: Billy's eyes were as big as saucers.
as big as saucers.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

took it out on.meaning: Treat someone badly because you are angry about something else.

took it out on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

rooted to the spot.meaning: Unable to move because of surprise or fear.
rooted to the spot.example: She stood rooted to the spot
rooted to the spot.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

about time.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

let the cat out of the bag.example: If he inadvertently let the cat out of the bag
let the cat out of the bag.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

out of the frying pan and into the fire.meaning: From a bad situation into an even worse one.
out of the frying pan and into the fire.example: Out of the frying pan and into the fire
out of the frying pan and into the fire.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

fallen under her spell.meaning: "Fall under someone's spell" = be charmed by someone, often by love.
fallen under her spell.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

acted my socks off.meaning: (Informal) "Do something your socks off" = do it with great energy.
acted my socks off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

the likes of us.example: won't talk to the likes of us
the likes of us.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

Sunday best.meaning: Your best clothes, worn for special occasions.
Sunday best.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

in spite of himself.meaning: Although something is true; not stopped by.
in spite of himself.example: Charlie yawned in spite of himself.
in spite of himself.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

it can't be helped.meaning: Nothing can be done about it.
it can't be helped.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

as if.meaning: (1) In a way that makes it seem that something is true ("looks as if it was struck by lightning"). (2) (Informal said alone) "As if!" = That is not true; that would never happen.

as if.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

rings a bell.meaning: Sounds familiar; makes you remember something a little.
rings a bell.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

so be it.meaning: Said when you accept something you don't like.

so be it.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

into the wrong hands.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

to the best of my knowledge.example: to the best of my knowledge
to the best of my knowledge.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

all at once.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

mind you.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

in front of.meaning: Near the front part of something; facing someone.

in front of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

so what.example: So what can I do now?
so what.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

chain mail.meaning: Armor made of many small metal rings joined together.
chain mail.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

look out.meaning: (1) To look outside from a window or a door. (2) "Look out!" = Be careful!
look out.example: Charlie dragged himself over to the window and looked out.
look out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

get on with it.meaning: Continue or start doing it, quickly.
get on with it.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

in the way.meaning: Stopping someone from moving or doing something.

in the way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

picked up.example: picked up a small can with two prongs
picked up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

on my side.example: I thought I'd almost got him on my side last semester
on my side.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

went on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

just you wait.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

as a result.example: As a result, Ezekiel and the Bloors were in danger
as a result.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.
